items.summary: Ukraine war briefing: Europe to join negotiations, says Kushner, as Putin warns against peace keepers  <font color="#
items.content:
US special envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff, meet Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy (centre) in Dublin. Photograph: Peter Morrison/AP
US special envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff, meet Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy (centre) in Dublin. Photograph: Peter Morrison/AP
Ukraine war briefing: Europe to join negotiations, says Kushner, as Putin warns against peace keepers
Jared Kushner says move will allow talks to address ‘broader postwar European security arrangements’; Putin refuses to soften territorial demands. What we know on day 1,724
Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include European countries , Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said late on Thursday, after meeting Russian president Vladimir Putin. “This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner ​said ​later on X. “We are also working toward ‌what would be the largest prisoner ​exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people ⁠with their families.”
After the Moscow meeting, Kushner and Witkoff flew ⁠to Ireland to attend a European summit and meet Zelenskyy, who said he was pleased at the prospect of European participation in talks and said he hoped the agenda would include steps towards a ceasefire and de-escalating the conflict . “We decided that we will work on an agenda about any kind of de-escalation, some kind of ceasefires,” Zelenskyy said after meeting the US envoys. “I hope that we will have such agenda,” he said.
Putin warned Europe not to send peacekeeping troops into Ukraine in the event of a peace deal saying it was a “continuation of war” . Putin also refused to soften his territorial demands and said Washington must work with its European allies to understand if they want peace or war in Ukraine.
Putin’s comments underlined how ⁠difficult the negotiations could become , given sharp differences between Moscow ​and European capitals over the way the war should end. “The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment because they are our partners and it’s important to us that they take part,” Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.
Kushner told Putin Washington had detected what he called “a big change” on the European side and was confident that expanding peace talks to include the Europeans would not hinder progress . Putin said Moscow had always been open to talking to the EU about Ukraine, but ​signalled serious outstanding differences. “As far as the Europeans are concerned, we have never been opposed to engaging in dialogue ‌with Europe, and we have never broken off that dialogue. It was ‌they who broke off the dialogue with the Russian Federation,” he said. “We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the US administration as a whole, to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” said Putin.
However, Zelenskyy said new restrictions were affecting the US-made satellite communications Kyiv uses on the battlefield , and that he found the US approach of discussing a new European security order with Russia “a bit strange”. Earlier on Thursday, he said disruptions to the Starshield satellite ​communications service had affected the entire frontline and Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine. Starshield is the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications service, and Ukraine suffered similar disruptions last month. “So far we know very little (on the Starshield restrictions). But some things are already clear: if someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then it tells us where things are going,” he said. SpaceX declined to comment.
During the talks, the conflict between the two countries continued . A Russian drone ⁠strike killed two people in the ⁠northern ⁠Ukrainian ​region of Sumy, Governor Oleh Hryhorov said ⁠on Telegram late on Thursday, while in Rivne ⁠in the north-west, ​five ‌people were injured ‌after a Russian drone hit ‌an apartment building, a local Ukrainian official said on Telegram early on Friday. In Russia’s ‌Belgorod region bordering Ukraine, a man ​was killed and another four injured in a drone attack, ⁠local officials said on Telegram ​on ​Thursday. Meanwhile, Ukrainian agricultural company Kernel Holding said on ⁠Thursday it had suspended operations at all its oilseed extraction plants ⁠following a ⁠series ​of Russian attacks on its facilities.

U.S. inflation outlook puts Federal Reserve rate hike in focus
As the final meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee looms on Dec. 8, inflation has reemerged as the Fed's bugbear.
Inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, and Fed officials are sounding the alarm.
Experts and traders see a 25-basis-point hike in December as the most likely scenario.
Kevin Warsh, chairman of the Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee meeting in Washington, Oct. 28, 2026.
At the start of the year, the Federal Reserve was sanguine about the American economy. Inflation seemed to be trending down. The shock from President Donald Trump's tariffs was abating. Economists projected the central bank could lower rates .
Instead, the Fed was forced to raise rates in September for the first time since 2023, hiking 25 basis points as inflation, which has run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years , reemerged as its bugbear.
As the Federal Open Market Committee's final meeting looms on Dec. 8, October's consumer price index was higher than expected : 0.4% month-on-month versus the 0.3% predicted in a Dow Jones survey of economists. So-called core CPI increased 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast.
Now, traders are certain the Fed will raise rates next month, according to the CME Fedwatch tool . The only question is by how much. Almost 88% of traders expect another 25-basis-point hike. The rest expect a half-point hike.
The cost of living has been a top issue on Americans' minds. Vice President JD Vance cited it as a reason the Republican Party lost so much ground in the midterm elections.
"We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said in an interview with "PBS NewsHour " on Tuesday, adding that prices are "on everyone's mind" and calling inflation readings "borderline disturbing."
Fed  Governor Christopher Waller said Tuesday that a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, adding this should be on the table if core CPI were "around 0.3%."
Christopher Waller, governor of the US Federal Reserve, speaks during the C. Peter McColough Series on International Economics at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York, US, on Thursday, Oct. 16, 2025.
"The latest CPI print strengthens the near-term case for tightening, even though a 25 basis point hike should be sufficient for December," Chester Liaw, G7 Economist at OCBC Group Research, said on Thursday.
Even with a hike, inflationary impulses could remain, Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at PGIM, said in a note Thursday.
With the Democrats in control of Congress next year, Trump could use executive actions to increase tariffs, Sockin said.
Since the labor market remains stable, Sockin said, he doesn't expect rising interest rates this year to derail "significant portions" of the U.S. economy, leaving open the door to future increases.
"We continue to expect the Fed to hike rates by 100 bps with the next increase coming in December and quarterly thereafter," Sockin added.

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett’s 6-Word Advice Is the Smartest Move You Can Make - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett’s 6-Word Advice Is the Smartest Move You Can Make  <font color="#6f6f6f"
items.content:
The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite have both slipped since the start of November, and many investors are uneasy about what comes next.
Warren Buffett's rule of being greedy when others are fearful helped turn his crisis-era investments in Goldman Sachs and Bank of America into billions of dollars in gains.
If stocks keep sliding, I think the move is to keep steadily investing in a diverse set of strong businesses and hold long term, because a market recovery won't lift every stock.
While it's been far from a smooth ride, stock market investors have had plenty of success over the last few years. Behind a booming artificial intelligence trade , the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.35% ) has gained nearly 115% since the fall of 2022, while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.39% ) has jumped more than 150%.
But the last couple of weeks have stung: The S&P 500 is down 3% over the past month, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 7%.
Many investors are uneasy. There's a lot of noise right now . It's natural. So, it seems to me that now is the perfect time to consider some sage advice from one of the most successful investors of all time: Warren Buffett.
Warren Buffett's advice for a stock market crash
Crashes happen in the stock market. They're a fact of life. They cannot be avoided, but what you do -- or don't do -- when one happens makes all the difference in the long run. It turns out that the latter half of one of Buffett's most famous aphorisms is one of the most important pieces of advice to keep in mind.
This simple phrase could help you avoid the costliest mistake you can make during a crash -- panic selling -- while remembering not to overlook the opportunity in front of you: the chance to buy shares of great businesses at a discount.
Buffett himself demonstrated this during the financial crisis. In September 2008, Berkshire Hathaway invested $5 billion in Goldman Sachs , receiving preferred shares paying a 10% dividend and warrants -- which turned into roughly $3.2 billion in profit. Buffett's $5 billion Bank of America investment in the wake of the crisis turned into a $12 billion on-paper profit six years later.
Of course, you have to be careful. Not all stocks are created equal, and crashes tend to weed out companies that weren't sound to begin with. Just because the market as a whole will inevitably recover does not mean that individual stocks will.
It's worth keeping another Buffett quote in mind: "Charlie (Munger) and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers." Investing in companies with durable competitive advantages, good economics that don't implode when the economy slows down or funding dries up, and led by competent leaders will help ensure the stock recovers when the dust settles.
I don't know whether the last couple of weeks are the start of something bigger or just a bump in a long rally -- no one does. But if stocks do keep sliding, keep doing what you were (hopefully) doing before: steadily investing in a diverse set of strong businesses and holding for the long term.

items.content:
Nvidia has lost $1.9 trillion in market value from its peak amid ongoing scandals with its now former CEO Jensen Huang.
Given Nvidia's central role to the artificial intelligence (AI) theme, heavy selling pressure could extend into other technology stocks.
Warren Buffett has straightforward advice for navigating uncertainty and volatility in the stock market.
The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has created outsize wealth for growth investors over the last several years. But one of its biggest winners is suddenly facing a crisis. Nvidia ( NVDA -4.34% ) stock plunged more than 12% during morning trading on Nov. 12 following news that longtime CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down .
The announcement follows reports concerning Huang's relationships with an executive at Nvidia as well as a businesswoman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's board of directors had launched an investigation into the matter.
CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the company evaluates a more permanent successor. I think Nvidia's troubles could become the catalyst for a broader stock market crash.
However, legendary investor Warren Buffett's approach to navigating volatility offers an important lesson about what investors should do next.
Why Nvidia's sell-off could trigger a stock market crash
Nvidia isn't just a normal semiconductor company. It's one of the world's most valuable businesses and a major component of the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.35% ) . Since the S&P 500 index is weighted by market capitalization, larger companies have a disproportionate influence on its performance.
In other words, if Nvidia represents approximately 6% of the S&P 500, a 20% decline in its shares would subtract roughly 1.2 percentage points from the index, assuming everything else remained unchanged. That might not sound catastrophic, but the potential consequences extend beyond Nvidia.
Microsoft , Apple , Alphabet , Amazon , and Meta Platforms also account for substantial portions of the S&P 500. Big tech is investing aggressively in AI infrastructure, making their valuations highly sensitive to changing expectations about the industry's future.
If investors interpret Nvidia's leadership transition as a reason to reassess the entire AI trade, selling pressure could begin spreading across other technology stocks. Due to their combined index weightings, a coordinated decline could pull the broader market significantly lower.

What is Warren Buffett's approach to falling stock prices?
When investors witness sharp declines in stock prices, usually their instinct is to sell before losses become even worse. That's not how Warren Buffett built his fortune. Buffett is known to welcome lower prices for businesses he wants to own more of.
The reasoning is straightforward: If a company's long-term earnings potential remains intact, a declining stock price can make the investment more attractive. Of course, the "Oracle of Omaha" does not champion indiscriminately buying every falling stock. His approach depends on understanding a company's competitive advantages , financial strength, and intrinsic value .
Huang's departure certainly introduces questions about leadership, product strategy, and execution. But his resignation does not automatically erase the strength of the underlying business.
Nvidia still has an extensive portfolio of intellectual property (IP), advanced GPU architectures, networking technology, and its widely adopted CUDA software ecosystem . Those competitive advantages have taken decades to develop.
The question investors should ask isn't how far Nvidia's stock could fall. It's whether the company's long-term earnings power has deteriorated enough to justify further declines.
I think the market may be underestimating the durability of Nvidia's business. During its fiscal second quarter of 2027, Nvidia generated $96.2 billion in revenue, increasing 106% year over year. Data center revenue reached $89 billion, up 117% year over year.
These results reflect historic investments by hyperscalers building infrastructure for AI training and inference. Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs and newer Vera Rubin systems are central to many of these projects.
Even if data center spending moderates, customers won't suddenly abandon existing computing platforms or stop upgrading their infrastructure. The same principle applies to other major technology companies.
Alphabet has Google Search, YouTube, and Google Cloud. Amazon operates the world's largest cloud infrastructure business through Amazon Web Services (AWS), alongside its enormous e-commerce platform. Meanwhile, Microsoft has its enterprise software ecosystem and Azure, while Meta benefits from billions of users across its social media platforms.
This demonstrates that these companies have substantial competitive advantages that extend beyond the latest AI investment cycle. This is why Nvidia's leadership transition, by itself, does not signal the end of the AI revolution.
Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 , giving investors an opportunity to evaluate its financial performance and future outlook. If the company continues delivering exceptional growth, attention should eventually shift back toward its fundamentals.
My prediction is that Nvidia's sell-off could lead to a short-lived crash as investors reassess technology valuations. However, I also think that any meaningful drawdowns could create a unique opportunity to buy the dip in financially strong companies at more attractive prices.
That's the lesson I'd take from Buffett. Rather than panic-selling because stock prices are falling, investors should evaluate whether their favorite businesses remain fundamentally sound. If they do, volatility could become an opportunity rather than a reason to sit on the sidelines.

items.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
items.summary: The attack is thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an open stretch of the Baltic Sea.
items.content:
Image caption, The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attack
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.
"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.
Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.
Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.
Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

items.title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
items.summary: The army has taken control of most of Tigray's main towns - it is unclear if the TPLF is capable of fighting back.
items.content:
Image caption, Pro-government forces marched into Tigray's capital less than two weeks after the war began
By Michael Teferi ,Â  BBC Africa Â  and Â  Yemane Nagish ,Â  BBC Tigrinya
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.
"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.
After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.
"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.
Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.
Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.
Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.
Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.
"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."
Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.
Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.
Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.
Image caption, Dozens of people were killed in drone strikes during the short conflict
He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."
The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.
It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.
Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.
Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.
"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.
Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.
The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.
Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.
Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.
Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.
However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.
Image caption, The army says it seized all these weapons from the TPLF during the fighting
Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."
He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.
Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.
Image caption, Most Mekelle residents only have money for the basic necessities at the moment
What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."
While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."
In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF . However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict.
"First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."
Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.
Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.
In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
Figure caption, Seven rebel groups from across Ethiopia have announced a new alliance
Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters.
"If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.
Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.
Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government.
However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence.
In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace.
"Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle.

Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Filipe Amorim/AFP/Getty Images
Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Filipe Amorim/AFP/Getty Images
Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week
Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Waves crash into a fort near Estoril as Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Zed Jameson/Anadolu/Getty Images Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.
Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.
Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.
A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

items.content:
Gold Rises Above $3,900 as Higher Treasury Yields and Fed Rate Expectations Weigh on Weekly Performance
Gold coin ©PIX1861 Gold prices advanced on Friday, recovering from a 13-month low reached during the previous session, although the precious metal remained on course for a weekly decline as investors assessed US inflation data, Treasury yields and expectations of further Federal Reserve interest rate increases.
Spot gold gained 1% to $3,915.31 per ounce by 03:22 GMT, but remained 3.5% lower for the week. US gold futures for December delivery rose 0.9% to $3,919.60, while a separate US futures quotation showed a 0.1% increase to $3,890.67.
Other precious metals also traded higher. Silver reached $50.0785 per ounce, while platinum increased 0.2% to $1,524.00.
Spot palladium advanced 0.3% to $1,001.40 per ounce, and palladium futures gained 0.5% to $997.00.
The US Dollar Index was largely unchanged at 103.21.
US Inflation Figures Prompt Reassessment of Interest Rate Outlook
Gold prices have faced downward pressure since Tuesday, when US consumer inflation data exceeded market forecasts and Federal Reserve officials indicated that additional monetary tightening could be necessary.
The figures prompted investors to revise expectations for the direction of US interest rates, contributing to higher government bond yields.
Treasury yields continued rising on Thursday, with increases exceeding 12 basis points across some maturities.
Shorter-term securities recorded the largest movements because their yields are particularly sensitive to changes in expectations for central bank policy.
Higher Treasury yields can reduce the relative appeal of gold, which does not provide interest payments. A stronger dollar can also affect demand by making the metal more expensive for investors holding other currencies.
These conditions contributed to the decline in gold prices during the week, despite the recovery recorded on Friday.
Federal Reserve Officials Support Further Measures to Address Inflation
Statements from Federal Reserve policymakers added to expectations of additional interest rate increases.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said on Thursday that controlling inflation remained necessary to prevent the economy from overheating.
San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly also indicated that further rate increases would probably be required, noting that inflationary pressures extended beyond industries directly affected by tariffs and energy prices.
Financial markets were pricing in a 25-basis-point increase at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, while some investors were also considering the possibility of a 50-basis-point adjustment.
Expectations of additional tightening have extended into subsequent meetings as investors assess the persistence of inflation and the resilience of US economic activity.
The possibility of higher borrowing costs has remained an important consideration for precious metals markets.
Oil Price Movements Add to US Inflation Considerations
Energy prices have also influenced expectations for inflation and monetary policy.
Brent crude approached $96 per barrel on Thursday following comments from US President Donald Trump concerning relations with Iran.
Trump said Washington no longer needed a diplomatic agreement with Tehran and indicated that military action remained a possibility.
The statements contributed to uncertainty surrounding Middle Eastern energy supplies and international shipping routes.
Higher oil prices can affect inflation through transportation, manufacturing and other operating costs, potentially influencing the Federal Reserve's assessment of future monetary policy decisions.
As a result, movements in energy markets have remained relevant to the outlook for bond yields, the dollar and gold.
ANZ Highlights Potential for Larger December Rate Increase
Analysts at ANZ linked gold's decline below $3,900 to higher energy costs, economic indicators pointing to continued activity, rising bond yields and the US Dollar Index trading above 103.
The bank indicated that these developments had reduced investment demand for gold.
ANZ analysts warned that "the Fed could even go for 50bp rate hikes in December" if economic conditions continued to support a more restrictive monetary policy approach.
The assessment reflected the possibility that persistent inflation and continued economic activity could influence the scale of future interest rate adjustments.
With gold recovering above $3,900 but remaining lower for the week, investors continued to monitor US economic indicators and statements from Federal Reserve policymakers.
The direction of Treasury yields, the dollar and inflation expectations is expected to remain relevant to precious metals prices as markets evaluate the potential for further monetary tightening.

Markets News, Nov. 12, 2026: Major Stock Indexes Fall as Investors Digest News of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Exit; AMD, Broadcom Soar
The U.S. stock market has been on a volatile run lately amid uncertainty about the sustainability of the AI trade that has propelled the market to record highs in recent years.
Credit: Michael Nagle / Bloomberg / Getty Images Stocks closed lower Thursday after a volatile day of trading, as investors processed the news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the most prominent executive in the AI era, has stepped down.
The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite finished the day down 0.4%, after falling as much as 1.6% in the opening minutes of trading, while the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average also closed 0.4% lower. The major indexes were coming off a winning session on Wednesday that was sparked in part by a rebound in Nvidia (NVDA) shares, which had plunged to start the week following revelations that Huang was being investigated by the company's board over an extramarital relationship he had with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% early Thursday—but managed to pare that loss to 4.3% by the close—after the company announced that Huang had resigned, effective immediately, and that CFO Colette Kress would take over as CEO on an interim basis. The news came after The Wall Street Journal reported late yesterday that Nvidia's board was preparing to dismiss Huang , who founded the company in 1993 and has served as CEO ever since. That report came on the heels of another by The New York Times that said Huang also recently had an affair with an Nvidia executive.
Shares of two major Nvidia rivals paced the broader market's recovery from steep early losses. Broadcom (AVGO) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) each climbed nearly 6% to lead S&P 500 advancers. Other chip stocks were under pressure, with Intel (INTC), Marvell Technology (MRVL) and Micron (MU) each down roughly 2%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) ticked lower after surging 6% the previous session.
Shares of a few of the companies that Nvidia invests in plunged today. CoreWeave shares (CRWV), which soared 25% yesterday following a strong quarterly earnings report from the cloud computing platform, fell 7%, while Nebius Group (NBIS) shares dropped 17% today after the AI cloud company released its quarterly results. Shares of optics and laser maker Lumentum Holdings (LITE) declined 4%.
Shares of Super Micro Computer (SMCI) tumbled 11%, following a report that the server maker and Nvidia partner is the target of a Department of Justice investigation. Bloomberg News reported that the DOJ is looking into whether Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who had the relationship with Jensen Huang, smuggled Supermicro products into China.
Meanwhile, Apple (AAPL) shares hit an all-time high of just below $360 in Thursday's session, before ending the day 0.1% lower. The stock has risen 31% since the start of the year, making it the top performer in the Magnificent 7 in 2026 year by a wide margin.
In other markets, WTI oil futures were recently up 2.8% at 88.90 per barrel after President Trump said this morning the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran. Gold futures were down 3.1% at $3,880 an ounce, trading at their lowest level since October 2025, while bitcoin traded at $71,500, down from a high yesterday of $74,700.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which affects interest rates on all sorts of consumer loans, was at 5.13%, up from its previous close of 4.99%. The yield has risen this week amid concerns that the Federal Reserve will raise rates again next month to tame inflation that remains well above the Fed's target.

Credit: Annabelle Chih / Bloomberg / Getty Images Supermicro shares were down 10% in recent trading and among the big decliners in the S&P 500. The stock is roughly flat since the start of the year but has lost nearly 30% of its value over the past 12 months.
Gold Slides, Dollar Risess Amid Rate-Hike Expectations
Gold prices hit a fresh 13-month low today as the U.S. dollar strengthens amid market expectations that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates.
Spot gold recently traded at $3,875 per ounce, its lowest level since early October 2025. The price has tumbled roughly 30% from its record highs above $5,500 early last year.
Since gold is a non-yielding asset, investors will turn to government bonds and other interest-paying assets when rates are moving higher.
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise its benchmark rate at its policy meeting in December in a bid to tame inflation that is running well above the central bank's target.
The drop in gold prices has coincided with a surge in the value of the U.S. dollar, which looks more attractive to foreign investors in a rate-hiking environment.
The U.S. dollar index, which measures the performance of the dollar against a basket of foreign currencies, was at 103.23 recently at its highest level since early April last year, just before President Trump announced reciprocal tariffs on U.S. trading partners around the world.
Meanwhile, the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which affects interest rates on a wide array of consumer loans, was at 5.11% recently, up from 4.84% a week ago, just before a strong jobs report on Friday and hotter-than-expected inflation data on Tuesday convinced market participants that more rate hikes are on the way.
Cisco, Applied Materials Due to Report After Closing Bell
Third-quarter earnings season is winding down, but a few notable reports are due today.
Networking hardware provider Cisco (CSCO) is scheduled to hand in its quarterly numbers after the closing bell, with analysts polled by Visible Alpha estimating that it will report nearly $4.2 billion in profit on $18.1 billion in revenue.
Analysts expect Applied Materials (AMAT), a chipmaking equipment supplier, to report $10.3 billion in revenue and a $3.2 billion GAAP profit after the close, according to Visible Alpha.
Shares of Cisco were up 0.5% recently, while Applied Materials' slipped 1%, with both stocks well off their intraday lows.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns After Days of Scrutiny
Jensen Huang is out—and Nvidia's shares are dropping.
Chip giant Nvidia (NVDA) early Thursday said CEO Jensen Huang, who helped co-found the company in the 1990s and had led it since, resigned—he also will leave as president and board member—effective immediately. The company appointed CFO Colette Kress its interim CEO and said it would "consider internal and external candidates" for a permanent replacement. Veteran tech executive Harvey Jones was named chairman.
Jensen Huang has been at the forefront of the development of AI around the world. Huang's resignation marks the latest twist in a whirlwind week, which began with reports that Huang was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy—the company later announced an investigation into the matter, and Huang publicly admitted to marital infidelity—and was inflamed by subsequent reporting that he had another affair with a subordinate at his company.
Shares of Nvidia, which had fallen nearly 10% this week through Tuesday's close, bounced during Wednesday's session but are now falling again. At recent prices, they are off almost 40% from last year's record highs.
The stock has been one of the stars of the bull run, with the company currently commanding the world's second-highest public valuation. That has lifted Huang's wealth and public profile, with his net worth estimated by Forbes as above $150 billion.
Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter financial results next week. That report will now likely be run by Kress, a former Microsoft (MSFT) and Cisco (CSCO) executive who joined the company in 2013.
Futures tied to the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 were down 1%,
and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures ticked higher.

items.content:
US Stock Futures Edge Lower as Nvidia Leadership Changes Offset Cisco and Applied Materials Forecasts: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street sign ©Rawpixel US stock index futures traded slightly lower on Friday as investors assessed developments surrounding Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), alongside financial updates from Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT), disruptions affecting Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) services and movements in commodity markets.
At 03:01 ET (08:01 GMT), Nasdaq 100 futures were down 74 points, or 0.3%, while S&P 500 futures declined five points, equivalent to 0.1%. Dow Jones futures were largely unchanged.
The movements followed the departure of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, which has prompted questions about the company's leadership transition and its position in the artificial intelligence semiconductor market.
Nvidia shares declined more than 4% on Thursday after the company announced Huang's departure following reports concerning his personal conduct and alleged connections to individuals associated with Chinese intelligence.
The allegations have also attracted attention from US lawmakers, although the reported claims have not been independently established.
According to Politico, Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott sent letters to Huang and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick requesting testimony in December concerning companies reportedly involved in transferring Nvidia's advanced processors to China in potential violation of US export restrictions.
Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent chief executive, with Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress appointed to lead the company on an interim basis.
President Donald Trump has also suggested former Apple executive Tim Cook as a possible candidate for the position.
The leadership changes come ahead of Nvidia's scheduled quarterly earnings announcement next week, when investors will receive updated information on the company's financial performance and outlook.
Nvidia's market capitalisation has declined substantially during November, with the source report estimating that the company has lost close to $1 trillion in value during the month.
Elsewhere, Asian equity markets declined, while government bonds in the United States, Japan and Australia also recorded losses.
Oil prices increased following comments from President Trump indicating that Washington no longer considered a peace agreement with Iran necessary.
Cisco Raises Annual Guidance Following Quarterly Revenue Growth
Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) raised its full-year financial outlook after issuing a current-quarter revenue forecast above analysts' expectations.
The networking equipment manufacturer reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of approximately $18.1 billion, exceeding market forecasts.
Cisco's results reflected demand for networking infrastructure used in data centres, including facilities supporting artificial intelligence applications.
The company has been expanding its AI-related networking products while competing with other technology suppliers, including Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Broadcom.
Orders increased 21% compared with the corresponding period a year earlier, although the growth rate moderated from 35% in the preceding quarter.
The company operates in a market where US policymakers are also examining the pace of data centre development, with some Democratic candidates elected during the midterm elections advocating restrictions on further expansion.
Cisco shares declined in extended-hours trading following the announcement.
Applied Materials Forecasts Fiscal First-Quarter Revenue of $11.1 Billion
Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) issued a fiscal first-quarter revenue forecast exceeding analyst expectations, citing continued demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The California-based company expects revenue of approximately $11.10 billion, with a potential variation of $500 million in either direction.
The forecast compares with the $10.89 billion consensus estimate reported by Reuters, citing LSEG data.
Applied Materials also reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of $4.16 per share, exceeding market expectations.
Revenue from its semiconductor systems division increased 64% to $8 billion, contributing to the quarterly performance.
The company supplies manufacturing equipment used by semiconductor producers, including those expanding production capacity for artificial intelligence-related chips.
During the post-results conference call, Chief Executive Gary Dickerson said 2027 would be "another record year for the market and Applied."
Applied Materials shares were slightly lower in after-hours trading, although the stock had gained more than 41% since the beginning of the year.
Microsoft Continues Work to Restore Outlook and Teams Services
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) said it was continuing efforts to restore access to Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services following a widespread disruption extending into a second day.
The company reported implementing additional measures intended to restore service availability but acknowledged that some changes had not produced the expected results.
"We've monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they're not taking as expected," Microsoft said in a social media update.
Users reported difficulties accessing several Microsoft 365 applications, particularly Outlook and Teams.
The disruptions affected customers across multiple regions, including Asia-Pacific and the Americas.
Microsoft shares declined in premarket trading as the company continued its recovery efforts.
Gold Recovers Above $3,900 as Investors Assess US Interest Rate Outlook
Gold prices increased on Friday after reaching a 13-month low during the previous session, although the metal remained on course for a weekly decline.
Spot gold rose 0.4% to $3,902.22 per ounce, recovering above the $3,900 level.
Despite the daily increase, prices remained more than 4% lower for the week.
The decline followed stronger-than-expected US consumer inflation figures and comments from Federal Reserve officials supporting a more restrictive monetary policy stance.
Higher US Treasury yields and a stronger dollar have also influenced gold prices, as investors reassessed the likelihood of additional interest rate increases.
Market expectations have shifted towards a possible Federal Reserve rate increase in December, with some traders considering the possibility of a 50-basis-point adjustment.
Investors were awaiting Friday's US Producer Price Index report for further information on wholesale inflation and its potential implications for monetary policy.
The release, together with forthcoming Federal Reserve commentary and Nvidia's quarterly results, was expected to remain a focus for financial markets.

S&P 500, Dow, Nasdaq Futures Recover After Markets End Lower On Jensen Huang’s Exit, Oil Price Pressure — CRWV, CBRS, NVDA, TSLA In Focus
The S&P 500 ended Thursday 0.4% lower, the Nasdaq 100 lost 0.3%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.4%.
Super Micro Computer stock tumbled about 11% amid a probe to find out if companies linked to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang smuggled its products to China.
U.S. stock indices ended lower on Thursday amid a leadership crisis in chipmaker Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down from his position, which weighed on overall tech and AI stocks, while elevated oil prices further bogged down sentiment.
The chief executive of the semiconductor giant resigned from his role after allegations surfaced regarding inappropriate relationships, including an association with an individual suspected by American intelligence of covert ties to Beijing, along with romantic ties with an Nvidia employee.

However, index futures were quick to recover after-hours. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 40 points. S&P 500 futures rose about 0.2%, while Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.3% at the time of writing.
The S&P 500 ended Thursday 0.4% lower, the Nasdaq 100 lost 0.3%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.4%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, ended 1.7% lower.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) fell 0.4%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) lost 0.4%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended 0.3% lower on Thursday.
Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF fell between 0.3% and 1% each on Thursday, mostly pulled down by weakness in Nvidia (NVDA). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) fell 0.1%.
Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for SPY, QQQ, and DIA all moved to 'extremely bullish' territory from being 'bearish' at the end of October.

Nvidia's competitors, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO), rose on Thursday. Fundstrat's Tom Lee stood by his view that technology stocks have already hit bottom. "We are sticking with the thesis that Technology stocks bottomed last week," Lee said on Thursday, in a note cited by CNBC. He added that Huang's exit "does not change our view."
More investors seemed to be of the view that Huang's exit could be a golden opportunity for other chipmakers or firms looking to design their own chips.
"This is a golden opportunity for Amazon, for Google, for AMD, for Broadcom, for OpenAI and Anthropic, who are hiring chip experts to help them design their own chips," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, told CNBC.
However, the case for AI spending reaching unprecedented levels, creating pressure on cash flows, continued to affect investor sentiment.
"The large technology companies are spending an absolute fortune on AI capex, and I think investors need to be very careful, said Sean Peche, founder and portfolio manager at Ranmore Fund Management.
"Investors tend to assume that what has performed well will continue to do so. History shows that isn't always the case."
Oil prices also jumped on Thursday, further weighing on overall markets after President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post, "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed." U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 2.55% to $88.74 a barrel, while Brent crude futures added 3.3% to $95.82 a barrel.
CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV) saw its market bonds climb on Thursday as stronger-than-expected corporate earnings earlier this week successfully eased widespread market concerns regarding the firm's heavy debt obligations.
Chipmaker Cerebras Systems Inc.(CBRS) share price rallied 13% after-hours after the firm reported record third-quarter revenue and issued a fourth-quarter sales forecast that beat Wall Street estimates, challenging market leader Nvidia Corp.(NVDA) as it wades through Jensen Huang's exit.
Federal prosecutors are investigating whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in efforts to smuggle Supermicro (SMCI) products into China, according to Bloomberg.
Investor appetite for Anthropic PBC's initial public offering has far outpaced supply , with orders reaching approximately six times the number of shares available, Bloomberg reported.
Shares of Tesla (TSLA) closed higher on Thursday after reports that merger discussions between itself and SpaceX are progressing and could lead to an announcement as soon as December.
Elon Musk's rocket and artificial intelligence company SpaceX (SPCX) said on Thursday that it plans for more than $74 billion in new U.S. supercomputing campuses, pairing a facility at its Starbase site in Texas with a second project in Cochise County in Arizona, as it seeks to expand its AI compute capacity on the ground.

items.title: If the Fed's Next Move Is a Rate Hike, Here's How a Long-Term Portfolio Should (and Shouldn't) Change - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If the Fed's Next Move Is a Rate Hike, Here's How a Long-Term Portfolio Should (and Shouldn't) Change  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The market’s counting on at least a quarter-point increase in interest rates next month.
While higher rates are meant to cool inflation by limiting economic growth, this cause-effect relationship is far from etched in stone.
While there are some proven steps you can take to protect your portfolio, remember that no two scenarios or situations are ever exactly the same.
If there was any lingering hope the Federal Reserve would be lowering rather than raising interest rates in the foreseeable future, it was just wiped away. Although the Bureau of Labor Statistics didn't publish an annualized inflation figure for this October due to last October's government shutdown, Tuesday's look at the month-to-month data confirms the United States' effective annualized rate of inflation still stands in the ballpark of 3%. That's not catastrophic, but it's certainly high enough to cause concern. The cost of borrowing money is elevated, for example, ultimately posing a threat to corporate profits. It's understandable if you're worried about your investment portfolio.
Just don't overreact to the rhetoric. While it's a backdrop you'll want to remain aware of, December's likely rate hike meant to curb these continued price increases isn't the tripwire it's being described to be.
Don't misunderstand. High and/or rising interest rates are somewhat correlated with an underperforming stock market. There's not an unreasonable basis for concern.
This correlation, however, isn't a particularly strong one. There are plenty of instances in which an inflationary environment that spurred rate hikes doesn't actually stymie the market, as in 2017 through 2019. And while the market eventually suffered a meltdown in 2008 under an overhang of high interest rates, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.35% ) rallied between 2005 and 2008 despite a steady pace of interest rate hikes throughout that period. High rates in the latter half of the 1990s weren't a problem for stocks either.
Perhaps the more pertinent takeaway about any historical correlation between stocks and interest rates, however, is the sheer unpredictability of interest rate changes. If there is a relationship between the Fed Funds Rate and the direction of equity prices, there's no discernible way to determine when either or both will reverse course. This poses the biggest risk that the matter will not be in the market when the economy finds itself back on firmer footing. The beginning of recoveries is often when the market makes the biggest gains.
In other words, knowing that you can't possibly know what you'd like to know, your best course of action is standing pat with quality holdings -- even if it means you know your stocks are due to suffer some degree of setback.
In this vein, for what it's worth, although the CME FedWatch data indicates traders are betting there's an 88% chance of a quarter-point increase in the federal funds rate in early December (and a 12% chance for a 50-basis-point rate hike), The Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee has also recently suggested the rate will also move at least a little lower at some point in the year ahead.
With all of that being said, although the possibility of rising interest rates in the near future doesn't mean you should get out of the market altogether -- or avoid getting in -- you might want to reallocate your portfolio in a way that's better-suited for such an environment.
None of these general rules for high and/or rising interest rates are etched in stone; there are always exceptions. Broadly speaking, though, there are four key strategic themes to consider if rates remain at high levels for a while.
In general, much of the growth of many growth companies is ultimately driven by borrowed money. If the cost of this funding increases or there's more risk to lenders, this growth potential is dialed back.
Plenty of value stocks are also dependent on debt, to be clear. This isn't a changing dynamic for these underlying companies, though, and unlike growth stocks, value stocks' price/earnings ratios don't expand as much when loans are cheap, and the economy is humming, only to see these earnings multiples compress when borrowing gets expensive again and the economy weakens.
There may be exceptions to the value-versus-growth dynamic in a rising rate environment, however. It's possible that some growth names don't depend on debt at all to drive growth, just as it's possible a more typical value name that's already heavily indebted and operating on paper-thin profit margins might still struggle in such an environment.
3. Own companies with real pricing power and products and services always in demand
It's possible, of course, that a company's balance sheet and operating costs remain entirely unaffected by higher interest rates. If an organization offers a service or product that's always in demand at any price regardless of the economic backdrop (think utilities and grocery stores), that outfit could conceivably shrug off any upcoming interest rate increases.
4. Understand how interest rate increases are impacting the economy in this particular cycle
Finally -- and perhaps most importantly -- remember that every situation is always at least a little bit different than any other seemingly similar one.
Take banks as an example. Banks' stocks are typically desirable when interest rates are elevated because higher rates mean more net interest income is earned on the same-sized loan portfolio. The current scenario is measurably different, though. Right now, higher interest rates are keeping would-be borrowers on the sidelines, preventing banks from making all the loans they might otherwise like to make. The Mortgage Bankers Association reports that in the final week of October, mortgage loan applications were down more than 40% from a year earlier and remained near their multiyear low set in the middle of the month.
At the same time, high interest rates continue to strengthen the value of the U.S. dollar. Although this works against U.S. companies that ship goods overseas, it works in favor of those that purchase a great deal of foreign-made products and services. If you look hard enough, you might find a buried treasure benefiting from this dynamic.

items.title: US terrorism case sheds light on RAF Fairford arrests mystery
items.summary: Suspect held in New York jail has been linked to handler behind Iran-linked operations in BritainWhen the US took custody of Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi in May, investigators hoped the string of terrorist and arson attacks he was accused of promoting and directing against American and Jewish targets in the UK and Europe on behalf of Iran would stop. They were wrong.An updated indictment, released on Tuesday by the US Department of Justice, describes some of what happened
items.content:
An armoured vehicle patrols RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. The US withdrew bombers from the base after a major security incident in September. Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty Images
An armoured vehicle patrols RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. The US withdrew bombers from the base after a major security incident in September. Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty Images
US terrorism case sheds light on RAF Fairford arrests mystery
Suspect held in New York jail has been linked to handler behind Iran-linked operations in Britain
When the US took custody of Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi in May, investigators hoped the string of terrorist and arson attacks he was accused of promoting and directing against American and Jewish targets in the UK and Europe on behalf of Iran would stop. They were wrong.
An updated indictment, released on Tuesday by the US Department of Justice, describes some of what happened next. It reveals that al-Saadi has two allies, believed to be in Iran, also trying to provoke fear and chaos in the UK, one of whom is accused of orchestrating the September incident at RAF Fairford.
Al-Saadi described himself as “a prisoner of war” when he first appeared in a Manhattan courtroom in June , accused of being the man behind a new terrorist group called Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia (Hayi) as well as a commander with Kata’ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi group backed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Yet, as al-Saadi awaited trial from a jail in New York, he was nevertheless able to make calls to his family. During the calls, according to the 26-page indictment , al-Saadi sought to pass on “coded messages” to two associates in Iran. On or about 24 September, he asked after one of them, named Ali. Ali had been transferred to the “international section”, family members said, as the FBI listened in.
Digesting this, al-Saadi gave an instruction – “Give him money so we can do it” – though it was not immediately obvious what he meant. In any event, Ali had already been busy, according to the US. Within days, Ali’s efforts had come together, directing the incident in a Cotswold village right next to RAF Fairford, the indictment says.
Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, told MPs in mid-October that the IRGC was “almost certainly” behind Fairford. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, added: “Our assessment is that it is highly likely to have been coordinated by a known individual based in Iran, and almost certainly directed by Iran’s IRGC.”
A fortnight later , two Britons from London were charged by UK police. They await trial, accused of assisting Iranian intelligence in breach of the 2023 National Security Act, and are yet to plead.
A photo released by US officials showing Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, right, with Qasem Soleimani, former commander of the IRGC. Photograph: Southern District of New York/AP Last month Westminster magistrates court in London heard that the men in the vans had been directed to drive to Fairford by a handler called Ali.
But it was not until last night that Ali was given a full name by investigators. The US indictment said he was Mohammed Ali al-Hassani, a 35-year-old Iraqi who had lived in Britain – it is unclear for how long – and was now using contacts and associates “to carry out terrorist attacks in the UK”.
Al-Hassani was said to be one of two associates of al-Saadi in the low-level campaign conducted by Hayi in March and April, along with Mohsen Mohajeri. A video obtained by US prosecutors shows Mohajeri telling al-Hassani: “We need to get focused on London” on 6 April, as they look at a map of the capital on a laptop. Six attacks in the capital followed shortly after.
In one case, all three men are accused of directing an individual in real time to attack a premises linked to an educational charity called Jewish Futures in Hendon, north London, on 17 April. Late that Friday, a man lit a plastic bag containing bottles of fluid outside the front of the building before fleeing.
Video evidence recovered by US prosecutors shows the three are linked to the individual via a FaceTime video call, its image projected on a large screen against the Hayi logo. During the call, al-Hassani appears to direct the perpetrator’s actions, telling them to take a lighter and “light one in your hand”, “light it” and “throw the fourth one”, according to the US.
The arson attack was basic, but the string of Hayi-linked arson attacks in London in March and April, on synagogues and other Jewish community sites, had a wider impact.
Roger Macmillan, a former head of security at Iran International, an independent London-based TV channel, whose staff have been the focus of threats and harassment from Tehran, argues it matters less whether Iran has the capability to kill or hurt people because “terrorism is not always about massive attacks, it is about instilling fear”.
Al-Saadi was arrested in Turkey in May, and extradited to the US within a couple of weeks. But al-Hassani and Mohajeri remained at liberty – and in August al-Hassani was back, this time accused by the US of orchestrating the preparations of the alleged plot against RAF Fairford.
It will be for the British courts to determine what happened at Fairford, but what the US indictment does demonstrate is that there remain other IRGC-linked individuals interested in orchestrating sabotage and terror plots in the UK.
Britain’s role in the US-led bombing of Iran may have been limited to allowing the US to use its airbases, but the UK has become a theatre of the now simmering conflict, a psychological arena in a war started by Donald Trump.

items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: What we know about the Microsoft global outage overnight
By Helen Davidson ,Â  Jessica Lamb Â  and Â  Helen Sullivan
A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products.
Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
Follow live updates: Microsoft scrambles to solve global outage affecting tens of thousands but says fixes not going 'as expected'
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".
Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.
The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.
The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.
Government agencies and services, including the Singaporean government and Australia's spy agency, have also said they have been affected.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.
Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.
The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do.
In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these.
On Friday morning, Microsoft said it was seeing "early signs of stabilisation", but service capacity has "not yet returned to normal levels".
In an earlier statement, the tech giant had said that its attempted fixes were "not taking as expected".
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.
"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Paul Spain from New Zealand-based advisory firm Gorilla Technology said that with e-mails and services offline, companies have practically "lost a business day", which is "frustrating" users".
