items.summary: Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs.
items.content:
Figure caption, How could the Nvidia CEOâs affair threaten US national security?
By Kali Hays ,Â  Technology reporter Â  and Â  Lily Jamali ,Â  North America Technology correspondent
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.
Nvidia has lost $550bn (Â£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.
Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.
Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.
Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.
How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.
A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.
Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.
Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.
Image caption, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.
Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.
Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.
Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?
Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.
It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.
Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.
Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.
Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.
The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.
Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.
But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.
Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.
Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.
Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.
Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.
Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.

Europe Enters Winter With Its Lowest Gas Inventory of the 2020s
Asian spot LNG is above $30 and EU storage was 71.6% full on Nov. 11, yet Rystad sees winter price risk running both ways.
The IEA's cold-winter case has EU storage below 10% of working capacity by end-March if Hormuz stays disrupted, and Qatar shipped just over 2.7 million tons in October against nearly 6.2 million in February.
Asian demand looks soft and US prices are cut off from the rally: China pays about $10 less than the Japan/Korea Marker, and the EIA has Henry Hub averaging $2.87 this winter.
Asian spot LNG is trading above $30 per million British thermal units and Europe is entering winter with its lowest gas inventory of the 2020s, yet Rystad Energy stops short of predicting a further rally. In its winter LNG outlook , published this week, the consultancy lays out as many ways for prices to fall as to rise and tells buyers to plan for a wide range of outcomes instead of one base case.
EU storage sites were 71.6% full in Gas Infrastructure Europe’s Nov. 11 update , with Germany at 58%, and that is well under the five-year average for the start of the heating season. The International Energy Agency modeled a cold winter combined with continued disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and found that EU storage could fall below 10% of working capacity by the end of March, S&P Global reported . A late cold snap would land when withdrawal rates, which slow as sites empty, are least able to respond.
Rystad says Europe will have to pay up to keep US cargoes from being pulled toward Asia, where the loss of Middle Eastern supply has buyers chasing the same Atlantic LNG. Asia is a less eager bidder than the price suggests, though. Rystad expects a mild winter in Northeast Asia, where LNG at $30 discourages gas burning and boosts coal use. Weather alone may matter less than it sounds. Bernstein calculated that a super El Niño would cut Japan’s winter heating demand by 19% but its LNG consumption by only 2% .
Price does more of the work. Bloomberg reported Monday that cheap domestic supply is curbing Chinese spot buying , with the national average LNG price near $22, almost $10 below the Japan/Korea Marker.
In the US, the Energy Information Administration’s Nov. 10 outlook has Henry Hub averaging $2.87 from November through March , 16% below last month’s forecast, with export terminals running near full capacity. Rystad expects a winter peak around $4, and both describe a US market cut off from the global rally.
October was both the busiest month for LNG tankers leaving Hormuz since February and the worst for attacks on shipping since the war began. S&P Global Energy tracking cited by Reuters counted 31 laden LNG tankers exiting the strait , up from 23 in September, while the Washington Institute for Near East Policy counted 37 ships struck over the same month.
Kpler data put Qatar’s October exports just above 2.7 million tons, against nearly 6.2 million in February. QatarEnergy said in March that Iranian attacks had cut 17% of its export capacity and has since extended force majeure through at least the end of December.
Supply from outside the Gulf has made up about two-thirds of the lost Qatari and UAE volumes since March, the IEA said, yet global LNG supply is still headed for a 3% drop this year, the steepest on record.
Transits stabilized in October, according to Rystad, and could allow a supply recovery by the second quarter of 2027, but output is “one escalation away from cratering again.” Diplomacy offers little to lean on. Iran’s top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, has denied that talks with Washington are under way and said Tehran will not let enriched nuclear material leave the country, while Washington insists nuclear concessions be part of any deal. European gas has risen three sessions running , with front-month TTF up 2% to €88.42 per megawatt-hour on Thursday morning.
On the upside, Rystad points to a cold snap in under-stocked Europe and an El Niño drought that would hit hydropower in Colombia and Brazil and lift regional gas demand. On the downside are the return of Middle Eastern LNG and mild weather in Europe and Asia.
A Gulf recovery by spring would help this winter’s math, though the IEA takes a gloomier view of the longer run. It puts cumulative LNG supply losses from 2026 to 2030 at 150 billion cubic meters, equal to 15% of the new supply expected globally over that period, and sees no meaningful relief before the end of the decade.

items.content:
Nvidia’s turmoil is prompting a rotation across chip stocks. Here's what we know
Nvidia's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its rivals.
AMD to Broadcom and even TSMC sees greater investor interest as they rotate out of Nvidia.
Nvidia 's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its biggest rivals, as investors bet that Jensen Huang's departure could loosen the AI chip giant's grip on an industry it has long dominated.
From AMD to Broadcom and even partner TSMC , chipmakers are emerging as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval, with market watchers pointing to a possible redistribution of manufacturing capacity and a narrowing of Nvidia's technological lead.
"What you're seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up," said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at Manulife Investment Management.
That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang's resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs including with a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy .
Huang's departure could give competitors an opportunity to close the gap as Nvidia navigates leadership uncertainty, Franklin highlighted, adding that the rotation was already helping fuel positive momentum in other semiconductor stocks.
Farzin Azam, managing director of equities trading at Mizuho Americas, said the shift was evident on trading desks, with investors moving toward chipmakers less exposed to Nvidia's management turmoil.
"Names such as TSMC, names such as Broadcom, names such as Advanced Micro will come as winners of this because they don't have this overhang of a management disruption," Azam told CNBC.
Nvidia shares have plunged 11% so far this week, while rivals AMD and Broadcom have gained 30% and 24%, respectively.
TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's most advanced processors, has also rallied 11% over the same period, as it stands to benefit , irrespective of which chip designer gains or loses. A rotation away from AI names perceived as risky also positions TSMC as a relatively safer play for those bullish on the overall theme.
The rotation away from Nvidia has also extended into less speculative corners of the semiconductor industry, including analog chipmakers such as Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Infineon, as investors adopt a more defensive stance, he said.
Texas Instruments has climbed about 13% this week, while Analog Devices and Germany's Infineon have advanced 12% and 14%, respectively.
Beyond the immediate market reaction, Huang's exit could fundamentally reshape competition across the AI supply chain, according to Dylan Patel, chief executive at semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis.
Patel said Huang had personally cultivated relationships with manufacturers and component suppliers, helping Nvidia secure scarce production capacity ahead of rivals.
That advantage could now come under pressure as companies including Google and Amazon strive to expand AI chip production.
The two hyperscalers were already gaining ground in securing supply-chain capacity relative to Nvidia, Patel said, and could accelerate those efforts without Huang's influence over suppliers.
SemiAnalysis' Dylan Patel sees Nvidia's grip on AI chip supply chain to weaken
"If Nvidia can't muster the supply chain, then technology is the only competitive advantage. And without Jensen, can they maintain technology advantages? Given they're only a year ahead of their biggest competitors, it's not like the gap is massive," Patel said.
The challenge is particularly acute as hyperscalers increasingly develop proprietary AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, while AMD and other semiconductor companies race to capture a larger slice of the market.
Yet the upheaval doesn't necessarily signal an end to the broader AI investment boom.
Franklin noted that major technology companies are projecting higher AI spending in 2027, with further increases possible in 2028, signaling the investment cycle remains structurally intact even as investors reassess which companies stand to benefit.
The bigger question is whether growing competition and the proliferation of open-source technologies eventually commoditize AI capabilities, putting pressure on chip prices and investment returns, he said.
For Nvidia, the immediate outlook may depend less on its earnings than on whether its next leadership team can reassure investors.
Azam said the stock appeared inexpensive relative to its earnings growth prospects, but warned that ongoing investigations and management uncertainty could limit any sustained recovery.
He expects Nvidia's earnings due Nov. 17 to remain strong, with investors likely to focus more closely on management's plans for navigating the crisis.
The result could be a reshuffling of winners within the semiconductor industry, with Franklin saying that investors were becoming more comfortable staying invested while rotating and diversifying their portfolios, instead of abandoning the market altogether.

items.content:
An overnight Russian drone attack hit a hospital in Kyiv. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian
An overnight Russian drone attack hit a hospital in Kyiv. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian
Russia strikes hospital in central Kyiv after SpaceX system falters again
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says speed restrictions on Starshield system made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down drones
Russia has attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said speed restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield system had made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down enemy drones.
Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building.
Meanwhile, Russia claimed it had shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest swarms sent by Kyiv. It reported that at least four people were killed in the southern region of Volgograd.
The blast in Kyiv blew out windows in nearby buildings including in the National Academy of Arts across the road. The six-storey hospital is located in the Shevchenkivskyi district, not far from the Danish and Romanian embassies, as well as cafes and a park popular with dog walkers.
Standing in the yard as smoke billowed from the burning building, and firefighters led dazed patients to safety, one witness, Oleksandr, said the attack had narrowly missed patients. “We were asleep when there was this massive boom. We all jumped out of bed straight away.
“There was glass all over the floor. People were running about … If it had hit a little further to the left it would have been much worse. We felt the shock wave.”
He added: “Targeting the wounded – that’s really low. Russia attacks everything. Where I live, high-rise blocks are being constantly hit by bombs. They don’t care where they drop them, or where they land.”
Russia has recently stepped up its strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, hitting power plants, passenger trains and two bridges across the Dnipro river. Ukraine says the attacks are part of a campaign of terror, designed to make a weary population capitulate.
On Thursday, Zelenskyy said the Starshield system – operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and overseen by the Pentagon – was again experiencing significant disruptions, after an unexplained slowdown last month.
He said some Russian aerial sorties had got through because Ukrainian interceptor systems that rely on the US satellite service could not reach the necessary speed to knock out enemy drones. Starshield is the Ukrainian military’s version of Starlink.
After the strike, firefighters led dazed patients to safety. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian The White House has yet to explain why the service has been throttled for a second time, but it comes after intense US-led shuttle diplomacy this week, with Donald Trump seemingly pressuring Zelenskyy to make territorial concessions to Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.
Trump’s emissaries, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate developer Steve Witkoff, met Putin in Moscow on Thursday. They then flew to Dublin to brief Zelenskyy on their talks, which came after trilateral negotiations on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi.
Kremlin negotiators insist that Ukraine hand over four Ukrainian provinces, including cities and villages Russian troops have been unable to conquer. They are also calling for a new “security architecture” in Europe – a demand in effect that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture, before eastern European nations joined the alliance.
At the same time, Moscow does not want European states to be involved in US-brokered talks to end the war in Ukraine. On Thursday, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said Europe had to take part since “US support” for Kyiv had ended.
“Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” Macron said. “At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”
Meanwhile, Russian strikes ⁠on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ⁠overnight caused ⁠power ​outages in 12 ⁠regions, said deputy energy minister Artem ⁠Nekrasov. The ‌affected regions are ‌Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Zhytomyr, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Kharkiv, ‌Khmelnytskyi and Chernihiv.
“Energy workers ​are working at an intensified pace, ⁠but new attacks ​and constant ​air raid ​alerts ​are ‌complicating and delaying ​repairs,” ​Nekrasov said.
In Kyiv, the orthopaedic hospital’s director, Ronan Derkach, said medical services had been temporarily suspended as a cleanup operation got under way. Thirty patients were taken to safety.

items.content:
The community of the Basilian sisters gather outside St. Joseph Monastery in Ivano-Frankivsk, Ukraine, after provincial visitation, May 2026. (Courtesy of Sr. Yeremiya Steblyna)
Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Email to a friend Print
I sat down to write this article and realized that I could not do it just then, because somewhere in the kitchen one of my sisters had to wash mountains of dishes alone that day. Before writing about being a superior, my first calling is to be one in real life. I quickly run down to the kitchen and get to work. Only later will I be able to return and calmly continue writing about what it means to be the superior of a large community in a country where drones fly every day, adults and children die, and our brothers, friends, or fathers sit in trenches so that the enemy will not seize our land.
At the age of 36, God called me to serve as the superior of a large community of 22 sisters. When I arrived here, I was the youngest sister.
Our monastery is located in the very center of the city of Ivano-Frankivsk in southwestern Ukraine. Because the monastery is located in the city center, many people come to ask for prayers. There are also those who ask for daily bread for themselves and their children.
St. Basil the Great, whose spiritual heritage Basilian Sisters live by each day, once conceived of the Basiliad. It was a kind of small town, a center of mercy. St. Basil the Great established such a complex in Caesarea in Cappadocia around the year 370. It included shelter for the poor, the sick, and travelers, as well as a hospital and school; at the very center of the Basiliad stood a church, a place of spiritual healing and encounter with God. It was not merely a charitable institution but an embodiment of Christian love: St. Basil saw Christ himself in those in need.
Our monastery in Ivano-Frankivsk closely resembles the Cappadocian Basiliad. On the one hand, the sisters serve and provide leadership at St. Basil the Great Catholic Primary School; on the other, they serve at St. Macrina's Day Center, a place for children who find themselves in difficult life circumstances, and they feed the poor who knock daily at the monastery gate. All these forms of service are united by our monastery church, where dozens of people come each day not only to ask the sisters for prayer but also to pray with us.
Related: I witnessed courage, resilience and resolve in Ukraine
My calling in this beautiful and holy place is to bring everyone together, helping this small group of very different women each day to remain a community: a place where Christ is not a beautiful idea, but a living presence among us.
To be a superior is to take into one's hands something very fragile: a person who has given her life to God. Each sister enters the community with the desire to love God and serve him. My ministry touches that profound desire directly. At my side, it can grow, mature, and become stronger, or it can slowly fade. Being a superior also means accepting one's own imperfection, fragility and weakness, which most often reveal themselves amid unexpected events, differing views, and mutual disagreements.
Being a superior does not begin with the right to decide, but with the duty to listen to God. A Vatican document about the exercise of authority in religious communities says authority in consecrated life is above all spiritual authority. A superior must support fidelity to one's vocation, remind us for whom we are here, and help the sisters respond to the working of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, my personal examination of conscience is formed by the question: "Are my decisions born of prayer, or chiefly of haste, fear, fatigue or the desire to control everything?"
One of my most important responsibilities is to make sure that prayer does not fade away in the community. Amid even the noblest ministries, we must not lose what is essential: time for worship and praise of God. Together, we have to reflect and discuss what time is best for communal prayer, so that all the sisters can be present.
As a superior, I am called to listen to every sister. Listening, dialogue and shared responsibility do not remove my duty to discern. For this reason, I cannot shift the burden of the final decision onto the community.
I am also aware that a community is exhausted not only by too much work but perhaps, above all, by a loss of meaning. This is why returning to our deep sources — the Gospel, our founders, our charism, and our history — is a guarantee that we will fulfill our concrete mission today. Some 30 years have already passed since the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church emerged from the underground, yet we still ask ourselves what in our life is truly Basilian and evangelical, and what we do only because "that is how it has always been."
For example, I asked the sisters to abandon the tradition of greeting only the superior on Mother's Day. It is not my feast day, but that of each one of us — women called to be spiritual mothers. After all, even in times of war, we as a community must learn to celebrate. There is a time to mourn life, and there is a time to celebrate it. And if God grants each of us another year of life or a significant event, this should bring every sister together around a shared table of celebration and gratitude.
Today, when Russian drones fly over our city day and night, it is difficult for me to tell the sisters that everything will be all right. When they wake several times during the night to air-raid alarms and go down to the shelter, how can I demand their presence at prayer? And what if eight children must also be brought to the shelter? Behind every such nighttime attack lie our fatigue, irritation, and feeling of helplessness.
In the midst of all this chaos, I understand that I am not "preserving" an ideal community. Rather, we are a community seeking Christ in this particular historical place and time that we are living in together. That is why it is so important for me to carry within myself the hope that the Lord is at work and present in the darkness and pain of this cruel war.
Finally, being a superior means, for me, remembering the sisters' birthdays and name days, searching for needed medicine even in another city or region, and having the strangest photographs in my phone gallery: an X-ray of a hand, a shoe size, newly born kittens, and the greens growing in our garden.
During these years spent here in the community, despite the difficulties, challenges, and war, I feel above all an immense gratitude. I realize how God loves me, but also refines me through every situation and every person whom I serve here.
This gratitude flows into my constant remembrance of the deceased sisters who once walked these corridors and prayed within these walls. It is gratitude to them for their perseverance and fidelity on the path of vocation, and for the prayer they now offer before the face of the Lord for each one of us.

“From a Launchpad for Chinese Companies’ Overseas Expansion to a U.S.-China Battleground”: AI Chip War Shakes Singapore, Testing Southeast Asia’s Diplomatic Balancing Strategy
Oliver Griffin is a policy and tech reporter at The Economy, focusing on the intersection of artificial intelligence, government regulation, and macroeconomic strategy. Based in Dublin, Oliver has reported extensively on European Union policy shifts and their ripple effects across global markets. Prior to joining The Economy, he covered technology policy for an international think tank, producing research cited by major institutions, including the OECD and IMF. Oliver studied political economy at Trinity College Dublin and later completed a master’s in data journalism at Columbia University. His reporting blends field interviews with rigorous statistical analysis, offering readers a nuanced understanding of how policy decisions shape industries and everyday lives. Beyond his newsroom work, Oliver contributes op-eds on ethics in AI and has been a guest commentator on BBC World and CNBC Europe.
Singapore, a hub for Chinese companies’ overseas expansion, caught in U.S.-China rivalry for technological supremacy
AI computing resources and advanced chips reach China through Southeast Asia as U.S. expands export controls
Southeast Asia’s diplomatic balancing act under threat amid pressure to take sides, particularly in advanced industries
Singapore, long a launchpad for Chinese companies expanding overseas, is facing direct pressure from the U.S.-China rivalry for technological supremacy. Amid mounting allegations that Chinese companies have secured advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI) computing resources through Southeast Asia, the United States has tightened regulation and scrutiny of the region’s data centers and semiconductor supply chains. Market observers expect Singapore and other Southeast Asian countries to face demands for clearer strategic choices, particularly in advanced technology.
On the 12th (all dates hereafter local time), Hong Kong’s South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported that a rapidly growing number of Chinese companies are using Singapore as a base for overseas expansion. Chinese coffee chain Luckin Coffee launched its overseas business in Singapore in 2023 and opened its 100th local store this past September. Milk tea brand CHAGEE has also steadily expanded its business since opening its first overseas store in Singapore in 2019. Similar moves are taking place in the information technology (IT) industry. Chinese online fast-fashion company Shein and game developer HoYoverse have relocated their global headquarters to Singapore, while TikTok parent ByteDance and Chinese-linked data center operator DayOne have also expanded their local operations.
Statistics confirm this trend. According to the Chinese government, China’s direct investment in Singapore totaled USD 16.9 billion last year, exceeding its investment in all other Southeast Asian countries combined, as well as its investment in the United States and the European Union (EU). Singapore’s Economic Development Board (EDB) also reported that Chinese companies accounted for 20.6% of new fixed-asset investment commitments last year, surpassing the United States (17.3%) for the first time. Several factors explain why so many Chinese companies are focusing on Singapore. Its large ethnic Chinese population and use of English as an official language make it easy for them to adapt locally. Other strengths include its concentration of multinational companies, stable legal and regulatory framework, and abundant skilled professionals. These factors have fueled the spread in recent years of so-called “Singapore-washing,” in which Chinese companies establish headquarters or corporate entities in Singapore to dilute their perceived Chinese identity and reduce geopolitical risks.
The situation has changed, however, as the U.S.-China rivalry for technological supremacy has intensified. The United States has begun tightening regulation and scrutiny of Chinese-linked companies based in Singapore. A prominent example is TikTok, the video platform owned by China’s ByteDance. TikTok established a global management structure by placing key executives in Singapore and appointing Singaporean Shou Zi Chew as chief executive officer (CEO), but failed to dispel U.S. national security concerns over its ties to its Chinese parent. Ultimately, in January this year, it established a separate joint venture to operate its U.S. service and transferred an 80.1% stake to U.S. and global investors, including Oracle, Silver Lake and United Arab Emirates (UAE) investment firm MGX. ByteDance’s stake was reduced to 19.9%, while operational authority and control over U.S. user data, recommendation algorithms and content management were also transferred to the new entity.
More recently, controversy has erupted over allegations that Nvidia’s advanced AI chips reached China through Singapore. At the center of the controversy is Huang Le (Alice Huang), who has been identified as having had an extramarital relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and is suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. Huang Le has been accused of involvement in supplying China with at least USD 7.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips through a corporate network built by her family, including Singaporean cloud company Megaspeed and China’s Shanghai Century Litong. On the 12th, the Singapore government said that although there was insufficient evidence to substantiate criminal allegations against Huang Le relating to Megaspeed, she had provided inaccurate information during the investigation and was therefore issued a stern warning and barred from reentering the country.
Market observers say the episode could also constrain Chinese investment practices in Southeast Asian AI infrastructure. Until now, Chinese companies have built data centers in Southeast Asia or rented computing capacity from Nvidia chips through local cloud providers to circumvent U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors. For example, in June last year, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that a Chinese AI developer had sent 4 engineers to Malaysia and rented about 300 servers equipped with Nvidia chips at a local data center to train an AI model. The engineers reportedly brought in approximately 80 terabytes (TB) of training data on hard drives and took the results, including model parameters, back to China after completing the training. In March this year, reports also emerged that ByteDance was working with Southeast Asian cloud provider Aolani Cloud on a project to deploy about 36,000 Nvidia Blackwell B200 chips in Malaysia.
Cases of illegal semiconductor shipments involving Southeast Asian countries have also continued to emerge. In February last year, Singaporean authorities charged 3 people, including Chinese nationals, with falsely declaring the end users of products purchased from U.S. server manufacturers Dell and Super Micro Computer. Authorities confirmed that the servers, which may have contained advanced Nvidia chips, had been shipped through Singapore to Malaysia, and also raised suspicions that they ultimately reached Chinese AI company DeepSeek. In August of the same year, the U.S. Department of Justice also arrested 2 Chinese nationals who had sent advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) through California-based ALX Solutions to logistics companies in Singapore and Malaysia before illegally exporting them to China. Investigators obtained records of at least 21 related shipments and also uncovered indications that Chinese and Hong Kong companies had paid the exporter.
Table 1. Cases of China’s Use of Southeast Asian AI Infrastructure and Semiconductor Shipments Through Indirect Routes
Use of AI infrastructure June 2025 Chinese AI company rents Nvidia servers at a Malaysian data center to train a model
March 2026 ByteDance pursues construction of Blackwell B200-based infrastructure in Malaysia with a local cloud provider
Illegal exports February 2025 Group charged in Singapore with falsely declaring servers’ end users and shipping them to Malaysia
August 2025 2 Chinese nationals arrested for smuggling advanced GPUs into China through logistics companies in Singapore and Malaysia
March 2026 Supermicro personnel charged with shipping USD 2.5 billion worth of AI servers to China through Southeast Asian companies and Taiwan
June and October 2026 Malaysian customs repeatedly intercepts servers equipped with advanced AI chips at an airport
Sources: The Wall Street Journal, Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs, U.S. Department of Justice, Malaysian customs
The scale of smuggling cases has grown considerably this year. In March, U.S. prosecutors charged 3 people, including Super Micro Computer co-founder Wally Liaw, with illegally shipping USD 2.5 billion worth of advanced AI servers to China. They reportedly shipped U.S.-made servers to Taiwan and Southeast Asia, repackaged them and sent them to China, even placing fake servers in preparation for on-site inspections by the U.S. manufacturer. Malaysian customs also seized 72 servers equipped with advanced AI chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport in June and intercepted another 30 last month. The servers seized in the two operations were valued at USD 12.93 million and USD 12.11 million, respectively. Customs authorities are expanding their investigation, believing the smuggling ring was involved in at least 5 attempts to illegally export semiconductors.
U.S. policymakers are also taking an active role in determining how American-made semiconductors are used. On the 4th, the Financial Times (FT) reported that Oracle had canceled a USD 7 billion AI chip rental contract with Tencent under pressure from the U.S. government. The contract would have allowed Tencent to use about 100,000 advanced AI chips at several data centers in Southeast Asia for 5 years. Separately, in May, the U.S. Commerce Department issued guidance aimed at restricting Chinese companies from obtaining advanced semiconductors through local subsidiaries in Southeast Asia. The U.S. Congress is also pursuing the Remote Access Security Act (RASA), which would expand the Commerce Department’s authority to regulate remote access to advanced semiconductors through overseas cloud services.
This tightening of regulations is expected to place a considerable burden on the diplomatic balancing approach that Southeast Asian countries have long maintained. Countries in the region have sustained economic ties with both powers, expanding trade and production-network cooperation with China while drawing in U.S. investment and advanced technology. In particular, after the U.S.-China trade war began in 2018, companies with production bases in China relocated factories to Southeast Asia to avoid U.S. tariffs, turning the conflict between the two powers into an opportunity to attract new investment. Recently, however, cracks have begun to appear in this strategy as the United States extends its controls to Southeast Asia’s advanced technology and infrastructure sectors. For example, under U.S. pressure, Malaysia introduced a prior-approval requirement in July last year for the export, transshipment and transit of U.S.-made high-performance AI chips. On the 12th, it also said it was considering legislation to oversee data center operators, facility locations and the volume of GPUs brought into the country.
Pressure on Southeast Asian countries over their strategic choices is expected to intensify further, as the United States and China accelerate efforts to build separate technology cooperation frameworks. Through “Pax Silica,” launched in December last year, the United States is reorganizing supply chains around friendly countries, spanning critical mineral mining and refining, advanced semiconductor production, and data centers and AI infrastructure. South Korea, Japan, Singapore and the Philippines are among the current participants in Pax Silica. In response, China led the establishment in July of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, an intergovernmental international organization headquartered in Shanghai. The organization aims to jointly develop AI technology, strengthen developing countries’ technological capabilities and expand cooperation in shaping international AI rules and standards. A total of 29 countries, including Indonesia, Laos, Russia and Pakistan, signed its founding agreement.

His reporting blends field interviews with rigorous statistical analysis, offering readers a nuanced understanding of how policy decisions shape industries and everyday lives. Beyond his newsroom work, Oliver contributes op-eds on ethics in AI and has been a guest commentator on BBC World and CNBC Europe.

Stock Market Crash: What History Says Comes Next After the Market's Big Single-Day Dip.
Earlier this month, on Nov. 5, the stock market experienced one of its biggest one-day declines in over a year. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) dropped 4.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) sank 5.5%. That was the market's worst day since April 2, 2025, when President Trump announced his import tariffs.
While the tariff-induced declines could have signaled a broader sell-off, they weren't, and the market fully recovered all its losses in just over a month. While this type of market rebound may seem unusual, it's not.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
In fact, since 1981, the S&P 500 has recovered from its 10-worst single day declines within two months, eight of those times. Importantly, the S&P 500 has also generated a positive return one year after these big market dips nine out of 10 times, with an over 20% return on eight occasions.
Source: Data shown is for the S&P 500 Price Index as of 12/31/25. Morningstar, Ned Davis Research, and Hartford Funds.
As such, history says that this market dip could be one of the best times to buy stocks.
On top of that, the market is entering one of its most bullish historical periods. Since 1938, the S&P 500 has risen in 95% of midterm election years from November through November of the following year. This period also tends to be the market's strongest stretch, with the S&P 500 generating an average annual return of 14.5% during these 12 months.
History would also indicate that a quick rebound could be in store. In midterm election years, the S&P 500 has produced positive returns in Q4 84% of the time, with an average return of 6.6%. The first quarter of the following year tends to be even better, with the market up 95% of the time with an average yearly return of 7.4%. The second quarter of the year after midterm elections also tends to see stocks do well, with the S&P 500 up 74% of the time with an average return of 5%.
It also doesn't matter much which party wins the midterms or which holds the presidency. That said, the combination of a Republican president and a Democratic Congress tends to produce the weakest market gains, with an average return of 4.9%. The S&P 500 has tended to perform much better when Congress is divided, with an average return of 17% when there is a Democratic president and a split Congress, and 13.7% when there is a Republican president and a split Congress.
History suggests a quick recovery from this dip, so I would be a buyer on this pullback.
Tech stocks were among the hardest-hit sectors with the recent pullback, as many newly elected officials called for a pause on the ongoing data center build-out. However, large hyperscalers already appear to have contingency plans, with the potential to shift spending overseas and toward Republican stronghold states like Wyoming. There is also the future potential to build data centers offshore, underwater, and then eventually in outer space.
In my view, the pullback could be a great opportunity to buy top AI semiconductor stocks , like Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD), as well as hyperscalers like Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN).
In general, though, I think the best core strategy in any market is to consistently dollar-cost average into index exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and if you have a little extra money on the sidelines, investing a little more after big down days is a great option. My top ETF to buy in this sell-off is the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100 index. This gives you significant exposure to the top tech names in the market. Meanwhile, an S&P 500-tracking ETF, like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT:VOO), is always a great long-term holding.

Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Edge Higher As Markets Attempt To Recover From Nvidia Rout: SLS, MSFT, CADL, MSTR In Focus
The chipmaker's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has stepped in as the interim CEO.
U.S. President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Huang should be replaced by Apple's Tim Cook.
Trump also said in a social media post that the U.S. doesn't "need a deal with Iran."
U.S. stock futures traded higher overnight late Thursday as markets reacted to a brutal day on Wall Street for Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), with the shares of the chipmaker extending its rout following the exit of its CEO, Jensen Huang.
However, rival AI and chip companies saw their shares rise as hopes of increased market share amid the Nvidia scandal boosted optimism.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
As of 09:37 p.m. EST, Dow futures gained 0.21%, while the S&P 500 futures were up 0.34% and Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.52%.
On Thursday, all three U.S. benchmark indexes ended the session lower. The Nasdaq Composite led the decline, shedding 100 points to close 0.39% down. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 lost 0.36% and 0.35%, respectively.
Despite the volatility from Nvidia's leadership upheaval, U.S. benchmark indexes are on track to post their best week since August.
The Nasdaq and the S&P 500 are headed about 3% higher this week, while the Dow is on track to post gains of nearly 2%.
Nvidia's CEO scandal continued to rock markets on Thursday, with Huang resigning from his position in the company following fresh reports of infidelity, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. NVDA shares have slumped nearly 11% so far this week amid the revelations and leadership upheaval.
The chipmaker's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has stepped in as the interim CEO as the board continues to scour for a full-time replacement both internally and externally.
U.S. President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that Huang should be replaced by Apple's Tim Cook. "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!"
Meanwhile, shares of rival companies, including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Broadcom Inc. (AVGO) gained nearly 6% and 5.5%, respectively, as markets are counting on them gaining higher market share amid the debacle.
AI chipmaker Cerebras Systems Inc. (CBRS) rallied more than 19% in extended trading hours after it reported better-than-expected quarterly results and also announced a new deal with Microsoft Corp. (MSFT).
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down 0.26% at close, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) fell 1% and the Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) declined 0.55%.
On the geopolitical front, Trump said in a social media post that the U.S. doesn't "need a deal with Iran" as "Those days have long since passed." He said that the U.S. had Iran's money and also had control over the Strait of Hormuz.
"I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.," he said.
Oil prices were marginally lower at the time of writing. Brent crude futures were trading at $95.77 a barrel, down about 0.05%, while WTI crude futures traded 0.33% lower at $88.45 per barrel.
Markets will now be tuning in to the U.S. Producer Price Index (PPI) for October on Friday. Economists polled by Dow Jones are expecting the headline PPI to rise 0.4% on the month and 6.6% year-over-year.
SELLAS Life Sciences Group Inc.
